blocks.text: There is a Ramayana in which Ravana gets his powers from Allah and the one who asks Allah for it is prophet Adam. It's in a Malay manuscript that has been at Oxford since 1633. Indonesia is world's largest Muslim majority country. In India we love to share that its currency once featured Ganesha. Its national airlines is named after Garuda and Ramayana is still performed across the islands. We call this as a proof of secularism. They became Muslim we say but they never let go of Rama. Then how did Allah end up inside Ramayana?

When Islamic rulers took control of these islands they realized they could not destroy Rama because before Islam Ramayana was everywhere in Malay archipelago. In Java local kings carved the entire story of Ramayana in two stone temples. Local poets translated the verses into their own language and every ruler was judged by whether he ruled with the character of Rama. The Ramayana was the moral foundation. So how did an island like this end up with Muslim rulers? Look at this map of Southeast Asia. Right between Sumatra and Malay Peninsula sits a narrow bottle

neck the Malacca Strait. The ships carrying nutmeg, cloves and silk between China, India and Europe had to pass through it. In 1400s Muslim merchant networks from India and Arabia gained control of the shipping, the credit and the global spice routes. They gave credit and lower taxes to fellow Muslims and simply sailed past the ports ruled by Hindu kings. You can see this trap in action with an exiled Hindu prince named Parmeshwara. Around the year 1400 he founded the port of Malacca. It was a tiny coastal settlement and the Muslim

merchant fleet avoided it because he was Hindu. So in 1414 he gave up the religion of his ancestors and converted to Islam and took the name Iskandar Shah. Now look what happens as soon as  he converts. Hundreds of merchant ships came to his docks and small outpost became the rich trading port in Southeast Asia. Malacca became the model for other coastal rulers watching this. The lesson was clear. If you wanted to survive conversion to Islam was price of doing business. With this wealth, the new coastal sultanates like Demak grew powerful enough to challenge and crush

the ancient Hindu Majapahit Empire in 1527. Java no longer had Hindu empire to protect its temple and its priest. Not everyone abandoned the old gods. As Islam spread across Java, some communities retreated into mountains in the east. One of those places was Mount Bromo, where they kept the religion of their ancestors. The hinterland remained devoted to Rama and their conquest stalled. For over a century, the Hindu interior fought back. In 1630, Sultan Agung of Mataram waged a holy war

against the infidels  of Balambangan, the last Hindu kingdom of Java. Many Hindu Brahmins and scholars crossed the sea to  Bali, and that is where the religion survives to this day. The sultans could capture the coastal palace, but they faced  millions of villagers whose entire lives were organized around Hindu rituals. These farmers did not live off foreign trade, so the boycott could not hurt them. So how do you rule an island where the rulers are Muslim, but the people still worship Rama? The sultans had two choices, and neither worked. If you try

to ban Rama by force, you trigger an armed rebellion. If you allow millions of subjects to keep worshiping a Hindu god, your Islamic conquest was never complete. So instead of fighting the story,  the rulers decided to rewrite it from the inside. The manuscript in Oxford is that rewrite. It is called Hikayat Sri Rama. The first big change is to Rama himself. In the original Valmiki Ramayana, Rama is an avatar of Vishnu. God descended on earth to restore Dharma. In this version, Vishnu is no longer the highest

power. Rama is Sri Rama, a king who wins only because Allah allows it. If they demoted Rama, what did they do with the villain? We all know Ravana gets his powers. He performs centuries of penance to Lord Brahma. In this version, Brahma is gone. Instead, the court scribes sent Ravana to a sacred mountain in Sri Lanka, originally called Sripada, a sacred place for both Hindus and Buddhists.  In traditional Islamic accounts, Adam fell to earth near Mecca, but Sripada was appropriated into Islamic

theology and renamed as Adam's Peak.  The manuscript places Ravana on this repurposed mountain, hanging upside down by his feet for 12 years, crying out for mercy. And who do you think hears his cries? The figure who answers his prayers was an Islamic prophet,  Adam. He takes pity on him, intercedes on his behalf, and begs Allah to grant Ravana dominion over  earth, sky, sea, and underworld. That's how Allah ended up inside Ramayana. And in this Islamic version, Sita herself sends Hanuman to pay his

respects at mountain where Adam landed. In another Islamic version, the Hanuman does not even stay a monkey.  He ends up as a human prince because in Islam, man is God's highest creation. And think how these stories impacted ordinary villagers. If Ravana's  powers come from Allah and Rama wins only with Allah's permission, who is the real supreme power in the universe? The scribes  did not stop with Rama and Ravana. In the chronicles like Babur Tana Javi, they wrote Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva into royal genealogies

as mortal descendants of the prophet Adam.  The gods lost their divine authority and became ordinary human ancestors. Christian missionaries had done the same across pagan Europe centuries earlier. Take the old gods, remove their divinity, and turn them into mortal men. But rewriting royal book was only the first step. The farmers of interior did not read manuscripts. They watched puppet shows to reshape how millions of ordinary people thought. Sufi missionaries needed to enter everyday village life. That is when they turned the village shadow puppet theater, the

Wayang Kulit, into a tool to spread the new religion. Before Islam, these puppets were drawn with realistic human proportions, just like temple statues. But the Islamic law strictly banned realistic human images. So the early Sufi preachers redesigned the puppets as abstract shapes so they could never be called idols. Even the performance became an Islamic lesson. The puppet master was described as Allah, moving helpless human beings. They kept the stories and the characters. They replaced Hindu mantras with recitation from Quran. The

Mahabharata was appropriated too. The local legends even adopted the five Pandava brothers to represent the five pillars of Islam. So what is left of Ramayan in Indonesia today? A giant chariot of Krishna driving Arjuna into battle stands right at the center of modern Jakarta. Today Indonesia is overwhelmingly Muslim and the people see Ramayana and the old epic simply as secular cultural stories. They no longer worship these figures the way their ancestors did. You can see this during harvest seasons in the villages of Java. Farmers pray at mosque and then

leave offerings in their rice fields for Devi Sri, the ancient Hindu goddesses of fertility and treated as a local folklore. So instead of fighting the old culture, they used the epic to convert them. For a villager whose hero already answered to Allah and those gods were already descendants of Adam, accepting Islam felt natural. The Sultans used Rama to win over the people. So what happened to Ramayana once it had done its job? The proof is in north of Java in Malaysia.  In 1991 state

government of Kelantan banned the public performances of this exact shadow play, declaring them un-Islamic. Once the population was converted, the stories were no longer needed. That was how an entire civilization was converted without ever knowing they were conquered. And in India we still call it a proof of secularism.
